mainEntity.name: SaaS developer vs freelance full-stack developer for startup project?

acceptedAnswer.text: A freelance full-stack developer can build a SaaS product, but a developer who specifically understands SaaS patterns — multi-tenancy, subscription billing, usage metering, admin dashboards — will do it correctly the first time. The most expensive SaaS architecture mistakes: building without multi-tenancy (painful to retrofit), skipping idempotency in webhook handlers (double charges), and building an admin panel that still requires database queries to answer customer questions. Hire a developer with specific SaaS production experience, not one who says 'I can figure it out.'

mainEntity.name: Which SaaS developer should I hire for multi-tenant architecture design?

acceptedAnswer.text: Multi-tenancy design decisions depend on your requirements: Row-level security (RLS) via PostgreSQL: simpler operationally, works for most B2B SaaS. Schema-per-tenant: better isolation, harder migration management. Database-per-tenant: maximum isolation, required for some compliance scenarios (healthcare, finance). The right developer asks: 'What are your compliance requirements?' before recommending an approach. If they immediately say 'we'll use RLS' without asking about your use case, that's a concern.

mainEntity.name: How do I hire a SaaS developer familiar with GDPR and data compliance?

acceptedAnswer.text: GDPR-specific SaaS requirements: (1) Data export API (every customer can request all their data in machine-readable format). (2) Right to erasure (delete account and all associated PII — requires careful cascade logic in a multi-tenant system). (3) Consent management (granular consent for marketing, analytics, etc.). (4) DPA (Data Processing Agreement) — a contractual requirement with customers in EU. (5) Data residency options (EU-only hosting for some customers). Ask candidates to describe how they've implemented data export in a previous SaaS project.

mainEntity.name: What is multi-tenancy in SaaS and why does it matter?

acceptedAnswer.text: Multi-tenancy means multiple customers share one application instance with complete data isolation between them. It matters because: (1) Operational efficiency — you manage one codebase and one deployment, not one per customer. (2) Cost efficiency — shared infrastructure is cheaper than dedicated per-customer. (3) Feature consistency — all customers get the same codebase and can be updated simultaneously. The isolation requirement is critical: one customer must never see another customer's data, ever. This requires either row-level filtering on every database query or database/schema isolation.

A SaaS developer with AWS and Kubernetes experience can design this migration plan and execute it with zero downtime using a properly sequenced migration strategy.

mainEntity.name: What is usage-based billing and how do SaaS developers implement it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usage-based billing (UBB) means customers pay based on what they consume — API calls, AI tokens used, storage, seats, or any other measurable unit. Implementation with Stripe: (1) Create a Stripe subscription with a metered price plan. (2) As usage occurs, report usage records to Stripe via the API (stripe.subscriptionItems.createUsageRecord). (3) Stripe aggregates usage within the billing period and charges the customer at the end. Key implementation considerations: usage records must be idempotent (with unique idempotency keys), usage reporting must be async (don't block the user action while reporting to Stripe), and customers need a real-time usage display in their dashboard.

mainEntity.name: How do SaaS developers handle customer onboarding flows?

acceptedAnswer.text: Effective SaaS onboarding: (1) Signup (email + password or OAuth → immediate account creation + tenant provisioning). (2) Email verification (required before full access). (3) Welcome email sequence (automated, value-focused). (4) In-app setup wizard (guide users to first value realization). (5) Trial activation (auto-start trial, show days remaining, prompt to add payment method). (6) Trial conversion (email sequence leading up to trial end, in-app upgrade prompts). Each step is tracked for analytics: completion rates, drop-off points, time to first value. A developer who thinks onboarding is just 'a signup form' hasn't built a real SaaS product.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between B2B and B2C SaaS development requirements?

acceptedAnswer.text: B2B SaaS specific requirements: organization workspaces (multiple users per account), SSO integration (enterprise buyers demand SAML/OIDC), SCIM provisioning, advanced RBAC (admin vs. editor vs. viewer at org level), invoice-based billing (net 30 terms, not just credit card), audit logging for compliance buyers, and sales-assisted onboarding (demo, trial, enterprise contract). B2C SaaS specific requirements: frictionless self-serve signup, individual user data model, credit card billing (no invoicing), viral growth features (referrals, shareable content), and mobile-optimized experience. Most SaaS starts B2C or SMB and moves upmarket toward B2B enterprise — the architecture should support this evolution.

mainEntity.name: How do SaaS developers implement SSO (Single Sign-On)?

acceptedAnswer.text: SSO for SaaS typically means SAML 2.0 or OIDC integration that lets enterprise customers use their identity provider (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace) to authenticate with your SaaS. Implementation options: (1) Auth0 (simplest — handles SAML and OIDC for you, just configure the connection per customer). (2) Clerk or WorkOS (managed SSO specifically for SaaS companies). (3) Custom SAML implementation (complex, not recommended). From a database standpoint: users authenticated via SSO are linked to their organization, their permissions come from your RBAC system (not the identity provider's groups), and you need to handle just-in-time provisioning (create a user record on first SSO login).

mainEntity.name: What are the key metrics a SaaS developer should track?

acceptedAnswer.text: Technical metrics (the developer's responsibility): API p99 latency, error rate by endpoint, database query time, queue depth (pending background jobs), and infrastructure costs by service. Business metrics (the developer should make visible): MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue), ARR, new MRR, expansion MRR, churned MRR, customer count by plan, trial-to-paid conversion rate, feature usage per plan tier. A SaaS developer who only tracks 'is the server up' and not business health metrics isn't serving the business well. mainEntity.name: How do SaaS developers handle database schema changes without downtime?

acceptedAnswer.text: Zero-downtime migration pattern: (1) Migrations must be backward compatible — the running code and the new code must both work with the new schema. (2) Add before remove — add the new column before the code that uses it, remove the old column after the code no longer references it. (3) Multi-phase deployment — deploy migration, then deploy code, then deploy cleanup migration. (4) Test on a copy of production data before applying. (5) Monitor error rates for 30 minutes after applying. (6) Have a rollback plan (alembic downgrade or a reverse migration). This is a non-negotiable discipline for any SaaS product with real users.
